items.title: Dolly Parton Says She’s Exploring ‘Avatar Performances’
items.summary:
Dolly Parton says she and her team have begun talking with companies that build "avatar performances," a possible workaround as health problems continue to keep her from appearing in person. Parton, 80, disclosed the discussions in an interview with People published Friday, Aug. 21, which Billboard subsequently reported on. She described the project as still in the "early stages of development" and offered no further detail about what form the performances would take.

Parton tied her current condition to the period she spent caring for her husband, Carl Thomas Dean, who died in March 2025 at 82 after nearly 60 years of marriage. "I am dealing with some health issues that I just didn't pay attention to when I was watching over Carl," she said. She also noted this is not the first such stretch, recalling that she was "down for several months with female issues" in the early 1980s.

The singer said the difference now is the volume of attention. "I think because we live in a 24/7 world with social media, everything gets magnified in ways it wasn't years ago," she said. "I used to joke that I was the Queen of the Tabloids, but now I guess I can say I'm the Queen of Social Media AI! Seriously, though, even though I'm still healin', I'm still workin'."

The comments follow a run of canceled and scaled-back commitments. Parton postponed her planned residency at the Colosseum at Caesars Palace in Las Vegas, moving the December 2025 dates to September 2026 before scrapping the run altogether in May. She has appeared only virtually at several 2026 engagements, among them the Academy of Country Music's Poet's Award presentation at the ACM Honors and the Aug. 14 dedication of Dollywood's NightFlight Expedition ride.

Parton has not mounted a traditional tour since 2016. At her first in-person public appearance of 2026, in March, she told a Dollywood crowd that grief had left her "worn down and worn out" and that she needed to rebuild herself "spiritually, emotionally and physically," while insisting her health had not slowed her work.

items.title: Janie Bradford, “Money (That’s What I Want)” Songwriter, Dies at 87
items.summary:
Janie Bradford, who went from Berry Gordy's receptionist to co-writer of "Money (That's What I Want)," died Friday at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles after an extended illness. She was 87. Her family announced the death, The Hollywood Reporter reported.

Born June 2, 1939, in Charleston, Missouri, Bradford decided to become a writer after the poet Robert Frost visited her high school. Living in Detroit with her sister, Clea, she befriended Jackie Wilson, who had just charted with "Reet Petite" in 1957. Wilson introduced her to Gordy, one of that song's writers, and she handed him a collection of her poetry.

Gordy hired Bradford as a receptionist after launching the Tamla and Motown labels in 1959. She sat down beside him at the piano one day while he worked on a song and added a verse of her own: "Your love gives me such a thrill, but your love don't pay my bills. Gimme some money, baby!" Barrett Strong recorded the result, which reached No. 23 on the Hot 100 and established the young company as a hit-maker. The Beatles, the Rolling Stones, the Flying Lizards, the Supremes, Boyz II Men and Charli XCX are among the acts who have since covered it.

Bradford spent roughly 25 years at Motown, later running writer relations for the company's publishing arm, Jobete. She co-wrote "Too Busy Thinking About My Baby," a No. 4 hit for Marvin Gaye in 1969, along with "Contract on Love" for Little Stevie Wonder, Mary Wells' "Your Old Standby," Diana Ross' "I Am Me" and the Supremes' "Time Changes Things" and "We Should Be Closer Together." She also wrote for the Temptations, the Four Tops and Martha and the Vandellas.

"Janie was there with me from the very beginning, before there was even a Motown, and she will always hold a very special place in my heart and in the Motown family," Gordy said in a statement. He described her as "smart, clever, witty and fun," adding that "she became Motown's first receptionist, but her talents quickly took her far beyond that desk."

In the 1990s Bradford founded the Heroes and Legends Awards, which over three decades honored music figures and awarded scholarships to students pursuing higher education. She was inducted into the Women Songwriters Hall of Fame in June. Survivors include her husband of 55 years, Wardean; her children, Lance and Nicole; her daughter-in-law, Carolyn; and her grandsons, Bradford and Austin.

items.title: See King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard Bring Out Max Weinberg at Queens Show
items.summary:
King Gizzard and the Lizard Wizard pulled Max Weinberg onstage during their Saturday show at Forest Hills Stadium in Queens, adding the E Street Band drummer as a second kit for an extended version of "Hot Water." Rolling Stone reported that Weinberg walked out with sticks in hand after being introduced by guitarist Joey Walker.

The cameo came about because the band's usual guest drummer was unavailable. Jay Weinberg, the former Slipknot drummer and Max's son, has sat in with the Australian psych group repeatedly over the past few years, most recently at their three-night Field of Visions II festival in Colorado the previous weekend.

Walker explained the substitution to the crowd. "In continuing with the tradition that we started over the last year or so, where we get our friend Jay Weinberg to come out and play a song with us. It'd be rude not to. But Jay's busy, he's down in Nashville, so Jay made a call. Alright, I'm going to call dad," he said, adding that they "got Max Weinberg, drove all the way from Atlantic City to come up and play a song with us."

Weinberg, a longtime drummer for Bruce Springsteen and for Conan O'Brien, drew a quick aside from Walker once he reached the stage: "I just got nervous." The band's Forest Hills Stadium run wraps Saturday night, and they play Under the K Bridge Park in Brooklyn on Sunday.

items.title: LMGI Awards Winners: ‘One Battle After Another,’ ‘Marty Supreme,’ ‘Pluribus’ Among Location Managers Guild’s Honorees
items.summary:
The Location Managers Guild International handed its top film prizes to the teams behind One Battle After Another and Marty Supreme at the 13th annual LMGI Awards, held Saturday night at the Eli and Edythe Broad Stage in Santa Monica. Comic and television personality Fritz Coleman hosted. Deadline reported the full slate of winners.

Michael Glaser, Michael Wesley and Rich Heichel took Outstanding Locations in a Contemporary Feature Film for Paul Thomas Anderson's One Battle After Another, which won Best Picture at this year's Oscars. Matthew Kania and Ross Brodar won the period feature category for A24's Marty Supreme, a Best Picture nominee. The Humboldt-Del Norte Film Commission in Northern California, represented by Cassandra Hesseltine, was named Outstanding Film Commission/Office for its work on One Battle After Another.

On the television side, the Apple TV series Pluribus won Outstanding Locations in a Contemporary Television Series for a six-person team led by Christian Diaz de Bedoya and John O'Connor. Mandi Dillin and David Park won the period series category for the second season of Fallout on Amazon Prime Video, and Paul Eskenazi and Joel McGlumphy took the anthology, movie or limited series award for Netflix's Black Rabbit. Alexandra Gibson and Christina Conway won the commercial category for the Toyota Trucks spot "They Don't Read Reviews."

Vince Gilligan, the creator behind Breaking Bad, Better Call Saul and Pluribus, received the Eva Monley Award, while location manager and production supervisor Mike Fantasia was given the Lifetime Achievement Award. The Association of Film Commissioners International took the 2026 Trailblazer Award, and the Environmental Media Association received the Humanitarian Award.

"Celebrating our LMGI winners was a truly remarkable experience," awards chair Nancy Haecker said in a statement, calling the evening "beautifully capped by the genius of Vince Gilligan." The guild represents career location professionals working in film, television, commercial and print production worldwide.

items.title: Bunny Levine, Librarian Turned Actress in ‘Gilmore Girls,’ Thelma’ and ‘You Don’t Mess With the Zohan,’ Dies at 97
items.summary:
Bunny Levine, the character actress whose credits ran from Gilmore Girls to You Don't Mess With the Zohan and Thelma, has died at 97. Her manager confirmed to The Hollywood Reporter that she died peacefully in her sleep; NBC Los Angeles reported that she died Thursday at her home in Tarzana, California.

Levine was born Dec. 22, 1928, in East Orange, New Jersey, and wanted to act from a young age. She set that aside for 25 years after high school, working as a school librarian while raising three children, according to her IMDb biography. She returned to it after retiring, taking classes and auditioning, and moved to Los Angeles following the death of her husband, Bernard Levine, in 2003.

The television work accumulated quickly from there. Levine appeared on Law & Order, Everybody Loves Raymond, Gilmore Girls, Ugly Betty, Private Practice, Criminal Minds, 2 Broke Girls, Raising Hope, Southland, New Girl, Getting On, The Mindy Project, Fuller House, Shameless and Dave.

On film she turned up in Slime City, The Jimmy Show, A Thousand Words and La La Land, along with the 2008 Adam Sandler comedy You Don't Mess With the Zohan. She worked with Sandler twice more, on Sandy Wexler in 2017 and the 2023 Netflix film You Are So Not Invited to My Bat Mitzvah.

Levine kept working into her 90s. Recent credits include The Invisible Raptor in 2023, Michael Angarano's Sacramento in 2024 with Kristen Stewart and Michael Cera, and Thelma the same year opposite June Squibb. She also appears in two projects released this year, the final season of The Upshaws and The Cure.
